analysis.one_liner: Requires pesticide makers to test for and report groundwater contamination and lets EPA restrict leaching pesticides.
analysis.headline: The groundwater-protection bill never got a committee vote, never gained a single cosponsor, and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced pesticide manufacturers to submit data on whether their products seep into groundwater, run monitoring wells, and report any detection within 15 working days to EPA, the state, and affected well owners. It would have let the EPA tighten or ban pesticide use around contaminated drinking-water sources, required states to write pesticide water-pollution prevention programs, and set health-based groundwater limits. It authorized roughly $80 million a year in federal spending for the work.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from private wells and public groundwater supplies, especially in farming regions, would get earlier warning of contamination, mandatory notification when pesticides are found in a well, and a federal backstop restricting pesticide use around drinking-water sources. States would receive federal grants covering up to half the cost of prevention programs, and farmers and applicators would get free site-specific information on soil and hydrology to guide pesticide decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rural well owners and drinking-water users

how_it_helps.text: Requires pesticide registrants to notify EPA, the state, the property owner, and anyone relying on the contaminated water source within 15 working days of any groundwater detection, so well users learn about contamination instead of finding out years later.

Creates automatic regulatory triggers: at 25 percent of the health-based groundwater limit the EPA must tighten the pesticide's registration, and at 50 percent the EPA must notify the state and can ban use in the vicinity of the contaminated drinking-water source if the state does not act within 180 days.
Requires states to develop EPA-approved pesticide water-pollution prevention programs with public hearings, and authorizes federal grants covering up to 50 percent of program costs.

Directs EPA to build a public information file on pesticide detections in groundwater and to provide states vulnerability mapping and technical assistance, and directs USDA, Commerce, and Interior to build information systems giving farmers and applicators site-specific soil, climate, and hydrology data.

Sets health-based groundwater residue guidance levels, defaulting to the detection limit when chronic-toxicity data are missing, which protects sensitive populations rather than waiting for proof of harm.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers would bear the cost of leaching studies, groundwater monitoring, management-practice development, and notification, and would face tighter or banned uses where contamination appears. Farmers would face certified-applicator requirements, sales and use recordkeeping, and possible county-wide use bans near contaminated wells. Taxpayers would fund up to $80 million a year in EPA programs and grants, and some of the industry's compliance costs would likely reach farmers and consumers through pesticide prices.

drawbacks.text: The triggers are unusually strict: a pesticide found at three sampling points is automatically deemed a leacher, any detection must be reported within 15 working days, and under the state-program section a registered use is cancelled immediately upon detection in a state without an approved program — a standard that restricts farm chemicals on the basis of detection alone, not proof of harm at unsafe levels.

Pesticides with leaching potential could be barred from county use after detections at just five locations at half the guidance level, and all such pesticides would be restricted to certified applicators with 30-year recordkeeping — real compliance burdens for farmers who rely on those products.

The bill authorizes up to $80 million a year in new federal spending ($50 million for EPA implementation, $25 million for state grants, $5 million for research) across fiscal years 1990-1994, plus the administrative cost of a new EPA-approved state program in every state.
Full registration restrictions are deferred up to 36 months while states write their programs, so protection for the most contaminated areas would arrive slowly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health payoff — earlier warning and enforceable limits on pesticides in drinking-water aquifers, which are expensive or impossible to clean once contaminated — plausibly outweighs the roughly $80 million a year in authorized spending. The costs fall mostly on pesticide registrants, though farmers would feel the restrictions in lost chemical options and paperwork, and the detection-based triggers in the bill are aggressive enough that a good-faith critic could call them disproportionate. The bill's fatal problem was not its design but that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to three subcommittees in early 1989, but none of them ever held a markup or vote, and it expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative James Oberstar of Minnesota introduced the Ground Water Safety Act on January 20, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, and Public Works and Transportation committees.

In February 1989 the bill was sent to three subcommittees — Agriculture's Department Operations subcommittee, Transportation's Water Resources subcommittee, and Energy and Commerce's Health and the Environment subcommittee — where the record ends.
Over the remaining two years of the Congress, no member of the House joined as a cosponsor and no committee or subcommittee took the bill up for a vote.
The bill died with the Congress on January 3, 1991, having never reached the House floor or the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided new leaching-data, monitoring, notification, and use-restriction requirements. Farmers also avoided certified-applicator and recordkeeping mandates, and states avoided mandatory program obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide manufacturers, who avoided new mandates

for.name: Rep. James L. Oberstar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pushed for a groundwater-protection framework covering pesticide registration, monitoring, notification, and state prevention programs; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded, and in two years not one House Democrat or Republican joined the Democratic sponsor as a cosponsor, so no partisan shape can be measured.

industries.note: Registrants would have had to fund leaching studies, groundwater monitoring, management practices, and rapid contamination notifications, and could lose registrations or face use bans where detections occur. Because the bill died, the industry avoided these costs; its interest ran against the bill's drinking-water protections.

Farmers would have faced certified-applicator requirements, sales and use recordkeeping, and possible county-wide bans on leaching pesticides near contaminated wells — but also federal grants, state program support, and free site-specific soil and hydrology information to guide application decisions.

industries.industry: Public water systems and state drinking-water agencies
industries.note: Operators of groundwater-fed water systems would get mandatory industry notification of detections, health-based guidance levels, and EPA technical assistance and vulnerability mapping, making it easier to protect source water. States would get federal grants covering up to half the cost of prevention programs.
